race.name: Brielle Day Hill & Dale 10K
race.venue: Brielle Elementary School / Green Acres Park
race.purpose: race competitively while protecting the larger Chicago build

preRace.headline: Hill & Dale.
preRace.subhead: Know the course. Run your race.
preRace.deck: The complete Brielle Day 10K plan: course, competition and an execution plan for every part of Saturday.
preRace.verdict: **Podium was realistic and a win was plausible, but neither was guaranteed.** Power governed the hills; pace described the result; symptoms retained veto power.
preRace.goalA: Execute within the planned power guardrails and contend for M50–59
preRace.goalB: Run an even, terrain-intelligent race without mechanical deterioration
preRace.goalC: Finish healthy and preserve the Chicago build
preRace.outlook: Aaron had current fitness to challenge for the M50–59 podium. Public registration contained 25 men age 50–59. Scott Isgett was the strongest known returning entrant and favorite; Aaron was the clearest known first challenger, with Joe DeSantis and Dennis Ehrhardt in the next group.
preRace.guardrails: The governing plan was controlled: 380–390 W on runnable terrain, brief hills no higher than 405 W, and no forced sprint. Sharp or escalating symptoms overrode the plan.
preRace.courseSummary: The organizer-linked trace listed 6.38 miles and 337 ft of gain, longer than an exact 10K. The course climbs early, returns to Holly Hill, rewards quick non-braking descents, and finishes downhill. Official time—not Garmin distance—would control the result.
preRace.fieldRead: Scott Isgett was the favorite from multiple Brielle results; Aaron entered as the first known challenger. Joe DeSantis and Dennis Ehrhardt were podium threats. Anonymous and race-morning entries kept the seed list provisional.

contenders.name: Scott Isgett
contenders.evidence: Four straight prior Brielle results; 35:16.9 at Belmar 2026

preRace.strategySummary: Pace could breathe with the grades, but competitive intent stayed constant. The best chance to beat the favorite was even execution: controlled climbing, free downhill speed and a decision after mile five.

strategy.cue: Accept being passed; the course rises early.
Settle in a compact group and run tangents.
Short stride, quick cadence; do not chase above the ceiling.
Recover over the crest and restore rhythm.
Hold effort through the return climb.
Quick feet, slight lean and no braking.
Re-engage, then let downhill speed come.

preRace.readinessGreen: Normal gait and stairs, restored sleep, rebounding HRV, ordinary soreness only and a normal warm-up response.
preRace.readinessYellow: Incomplete recovery or heavy legs with normal gait and symptoms no worse than 0–2/10: run controlled and reduce the day.
preRace.readinessRed: Sharp or increasing pain, gait change, illness, dizziness, abnormal fatigue or another severely short night: no hard race.

logistics.item: Park legally off Highway 71 before Union Lane closure.
Bathroom, kit and final readiness check.
Brisk walk, activation and non-running mobility.

preRace.bibPickup: Race-day pickup and late online registration 7:30–8:45 AM at Green Acres Park; advance pickup Thursday and Friday.
preRace.parking: Legal side streets off Highway 71; no parking on Schoolhouse Road. Union Lane expected to close around 8:00 AM.
preRace.arrival: Target 7:20–7:30 AM, before traffic controls tighten.
preRace.warmup: Brisk walking, ankle/hip/glute activation and mobility; no extra running beyond the planned session.
preRace.fuel: 60–90 g breakfast carbohydrate; familiar pre-start gel
preRace.hydration: 12–16 oz sodium fluid by 7:45; optional course water
preRace.equipmentNotes: Garmin screen: three-second power, lap-average power, lap pace and HR. One-mile auto-lap. No narrow pace alerts.

postRace.headline: A disrupting force
postRace.deck: Aaron Greenwood arrived ready to race, trusted the feeling, and turned the hardest 10K course of his season into a decisive age-group victory and a new official event best.
postRace.verdict: **This was a breakthrough, not a fluke.** Aaron absorbed two major late climbs, closed the final 0.48 mile near 6:15 per mile, and produced his best mechanics at the finish.
postRace.resultSummary: At age 53, Aaron ran **44:11.6** on a relentlessly rolling course and won Male 50–59 by **2 minutes, 38.8 seconds**. He finished **19th of 202 overall** and **16th of 119 men**.
postRace.recordNote: Brielle was **2:07.95 faster** than the 46:19.55 Revolutionary Run result. Because Brielle's course certification has not been verified, the careful label is **official 10K event best**; Revolutionary Run remains the certified-road benchmark.
postRace.resultQuote: He arrived as the leading challenger. He left as the class of the age group.
postRace.fieldRead: The pre-race favorite finished second. Aaron reversed the expected order and won decisively. Third and fourth were separated by three-tenths; Aaron was nearly three minutes clear of that fight.
postRace.executionSummary: Brielle punished rigid pace targets. Aaron allowed pace to change with the terrain while preserving competitive output, then accessed his fastest decisive running after the final major climb.

splits.note: Assertive opening climb; HR still in early kinetics.
Pace slowed appropriately while output stayed competitive.
Recovered speed immediately after the climb.
Still generating force at race-defining intensity.
Best decisive running came after the hills.

postRace.executionDiagnosis: Heart rate rose progressively instead of spiking and collapsing. Garmin's 5.0 aerobic Training Effect represents a maximal race-sized stimulus requiring recovery, not a failed effort.
postRace.aerobicDiagnosis: Aaron averaged 162 bpm for 44 minutes, reached the upper 160s late, and still closed. The pattern supports a **large, usable aerobic engine** with enough lactate processing and oxygen delivery to sustain competitive output across a hilly 10K.
postRace.formDiagnosis: This was the opposite of mechanical collapse. As Aaron accelerated, contact time shortened, stride length opened and proportional vertical movement fell.
postRace.subjective: Showed up fresh, decided to race, felt excellent and finished feeling the decision was right.
postRace.pain: No injury and no unusual leg or hip strain during the race.
whatWorked: **Accumulated fitness.** Months of speed, threshold, hills and endurance created the result.
**Permission to race.** Aaron arrived fresh and made a clean decision to compete.
**Shoe confidence.** He chose the trusted ASICS Metaspeed Sky Tokyo.
**Terrain intelligence.** Pace breathed with elevation while intent stayed constant.
**Late-race speed.** Cadence and stride were still available after 40 minutes.
**Healthy movement.** No pain or protective loading was reported.
opportunities: **Climbing economy.** Preserve quick contact and forward projection as force rises.
**Moderate-pace economy.** Make race-speed organization cheaper at marathon and steady paces.
**Long-duration durability.** Carry mechanics, fueling and tissue resilience beyond two hours.
**Start calibration.** Spend slightly less in the opening minutes on flatter championship courses.
**Upper-body economy.** Loose jaw, shoulders down, elbows back and hands in lane.

postRace.progressionSummary: The mile, 5K, half-marathon and 10K results demonstrate multiple kinds of ability rather than one fortunate distance or day.

futureGoals.label: IMMEDIATE
futureGoals.title: Sub-20 5K
futureGoals.text: Nine seconds separate Aaron from the mark. It is a present-tense goal.

futureGoals.label: NEXT 10K
futureGoals.title: Sub-43
futureGoals.text: A flatter certified course makes this defensible; sub-42 is the stretch beyond it.

futureGoals.label: HALF MARATHON
futureGoals.title: 1:42, then sub-1:40
futureGoals.text: The bridge is sustainable threshold work and durability.

futureGoals.label: CHICAGO
futureGoals.title: Sub-4 remains credible
futureGoals.text: Brielle strengthens aerobic confidence without proving 26.2-mile durability by itself.

postRace.futureSummary: At 53, Aaron is still harvesting adaptations from a relatively young training age. If health, recovery and consistency remain protected, improvement over the next **one to three seasons** is realistic.
postRace.nextStep: Respect the race-sized load, recover fully, and return to Chicago-specific durability without trying to repay missed miles.
